beats.narration: Begin by framing Foundations of Computational Thinking as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Consider this worked case: A student breaks down a sorting problem into identifying the input list, comparing elements, and arranging them in order before writing pseudo-code. On screen, display a split screen: left side shows a messy real-world problem, right side shows a clean pseudo-code block with labeled abstraction and decomposition steps. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Foundations of Computational Thinking
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a split screen: left side shows a messy real-world problem, right side shows a clean pseudo-code block with labeled abstraction and decomposition steps.

beats.narration: Now define Pseudo-Code and Language Expression precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Consider this worked case: A pseudo-code function for finding the maximum value in a list is converted to Python, preserving the logical flow while adding syntax and type constraints. On screen, show a side-by-side comparison of the pseudo-code and Python implementation, highlighting how each pseudo-code line maps to a specific Python statement. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Pseudo-Code and Language Expression
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison of the pseudo-code and Python implementation, highlighting how each pseudo-code line maps to a specific Python statement.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Elementary Data Structures: Lists operates in a concrete sequence. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Consider this worked case: A student uses a Python list to store test scores, then iterates through it to calculate the average using a simple loop. On screen, animate a list growing with each new score added, then show a pointer moving through the list to demonstrate sequential access during iteration. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Lists
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Animate a list growing with each new score added, then show a pointer moving through the list to demonstrate sequential access during iteration.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Elementary Data Structures: Trees and make the decision criteria explicit. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Consider this worked case: A binary tree represents a file system where directories are nodes and files are leaf nodes, allowing efficient path resolution. On screen, render a binary tree diagram with labeled parent-child links, highlighting how a search path branches down to a target leaf node. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Trees
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a binary tree diagram with labeled parent-child links, highlighting how a search path branches down to a target leaf node.

beats.narration: Apply Elementary Data Structures: Graphs to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Consider this worked case: A student models a city's road network as a graph where intersections are nodes and roads are edges to find the shortest path. On screen, draw a simple graph with labeled nodes and directed edges, then trace a path from a start node to an end node using a step-by-step animation. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Graphs
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a simple graph with labeled nodes and directed edges, then trace a path from a start node to an end node using a step-by-step animation.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Recursive Problem Solving, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. Consider this worked case: A factorial function calculates n! by multiplying n with the result of factorial(n-1), stopping when n equals 1. On screen, show a recursive call stack expanding downward with each function call, then collapsing upward as base cases return values. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Recursive Problem Solving
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a recursive call stack expanding downward with each function call, then collapsing upward as base cases return values.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Debugging and Testing Protocols with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns. Consider this worked case: A student uses print statements and a test harness to verify that a sorting algorithm correctly handles edge cases like empty lists or single-element lists. On screen, display a debugger interface highlighting a runtime error, then show a test suite passing/failing based on input/output contracts. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Debugging and Testing Protocols
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a debugger interface highlighting a runtime error, then show a test suite passing/failing based on input/output contracts.

beats.narration: Use State and Control Flow Management to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. Consider this worked case: A student defines a class with explicit attributes and methods, ensuring that each method updates state according to a documented contract. On screen, show a state machine diagram transitioning between states, with arrows labeled by method calls and state updates. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: State and Control Flow Management
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a state machine diagram transitioning between states, with arrows labeled by method calls and state updates.

beats.narration: Connect Verification and Local Expander Preparation to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Consider this worked case: A student cross-references the pseudo-code implementation with the source excerpts, ensuring that terms like 'basic blocks', 'terminator instruction', and 'namespace' are correctly applied. On screen, display a checklist overlay with checkboxes for each source ID, technical term reuse, and claim verification, ready for the local expander to generate full narration. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Verification and Local Expander Preparation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist overlay with checkboxes for each source ID, technical term reuse, and claim verification, ready for the local expander to generate full narration.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Consider this worked case: A student reviews their assignment against the checklist, confirming that pseudo-code and code match, data structures are correctly implemented, recursion is applied, and tests pass. On screen, show a clean, printable checklist with sections for each beat, checkboxes for claim verification, and space for instructor notes. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a clean, printable checklist with sections for each beat, checkboxes for claim verification, and space for instructor notes.

sources.excerpt: LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. A module contains global values, functions, declarations, and metadata. A function contains basic blocks, and every basic block ends with a terminator instruction. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.
